#3661. GTA 6 Players Hate Using ATMs: ‘Just Let Me Type In A Number!”

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally out on PlayStation and Xbox. So, I’ve been watching my friends play it, which has been a blast. And all of them are loving the game, but one annoying bit of the massive game that they all seem to hate is using ATMs. And it’s not just them. A lot of people online desperately want the ATMs improved in GTA 6.

Money plays a big part in Grand Theft Auto 6. And for much of the game’s runtime, you’ll be counting dollars carefully as you save what you can and spend cautiously. Part of this loop also involves putting loose cash into your bank account via ATMs. If you don’t do that, you can lose much of it when you die or get arrested. So it is important to put it into your bank and savings account. Yet, for some odd, confounding reason, Rockstar has made the act of depositing and withdrawing money from an ATM very annoying.

If you haven’t played GTA 6,Â you might just assume you go to an ATM and type in how much you want to take out or put in. Nope! Instead, you have to hold different shoulder buttons on the controller to scroll through how much you want to deposit or withdraw. And this scrolling function starts to speed up very quickly, often leading to me blowing past the amount I wanted and having to slowly scroll back, sometimes missing it again. It sucks!

“I’m loving this game, but why can’t I just type in fucking number on the ATM, dude,” asked one of my friends in a PlayStation party chat last night. I had no good answer.

Others online are also confused and annoyed by the ATM controls.

“This right here is my biggest gripe so far. Let me type in a number, JUST LIKE PUTTING JN THE STUPID CODES,” posted one user on Reddit.

“I’m amazed more people aren’t pissed at using L1/R1 to withdraw/deposit. Like, just let me type it in,” said someone else.

“1, 2, 3, 4, …10, 20, 30, … 300, 400, … 10 000, 20 000, 30 000! … Fuck… I just wanted to withdraw 500,” complained a GTA 6 player.

“Dude, I spent straight up 2 minutes trying to withdraw [exactly] $900… It was so fucking annoying,” shared a user on the GTA 6 subreddit.

“It blows my mind that something this small wasn’t implemented over the course of development. Them keeping the exact same system as Red Dead Redemption 2 is extremely flawed in a game like this; I would honestly prefer the ATM mechanics of GTA V over what we got in this game,” explained someone in a Reddit post titled: My biggest complaint with this game.

That last comment brings up a good point and one which makes this all the more confusing to me. In GTA V and GTA Online, there are pre-selected amounts you select, like $100 or $1,000, that make banking easier. Not perfect, but it is so much better and easier than GTA 6‘s ATM controls that I’m genuinely confused as to why Rockstar didn’t just… do that.

In a game that tries (and often succeeds) to recreate as many small details of real life in a digital world as possible, including shirts getting damp with sweat and accurate reflections, it’s strange that Rockstar invented a new, terrible way to interact with an ATM.

New arrivals are landing in the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog this month, but at the same time, you can also expect a few departures from that gaming library. PlayStation Plus Game Catalog games leaving soon

  • Granblue Fantasy Relink
  • Somerville

While the story isn't much to write home about, it's the gameplay and worldbuilding where this Granblue spin-off shines, and it got even better earlier this year with the Endless Ragnarok expansion.

#3659. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3656. Despite The Pricing Hellscape, Console Sales Grew In October

Video game consoles are more expensive than ever, but sales are growing regardless, at least in the US.

Circana has released its report for US video game industry sales in October, confirming that PS5 unit sales increased by 5% compared to October 2025. That's despite the average selling price of a PS5 increasing by 13%.

Xbox Series X|S unit sales jumped by 10% in October 2026 compared to October 2025, and the average selling price rose by 29% year-over-year. The Switch 2 was October 2026's top console in unit and dollar sales, and it remains 2026's best-performing console by those measurements, followed by PS5. However, Circana did not break out the specifics for Switch 2 unit sales or average selling price changes.

Total hardware spending in the US on game consoles was up by 2%, reaching $357 million. Higher pricing drove the dollar sales growth, Circana said, noting that PS5 dollar sales rose by 20% and Xbox Series X|S jumped by 42%. However, Switch 2 sales, measured by dollar sales, fell by 11%.

Looking back to September 2026, PS5 hardware dollar sales grew by 43%, while spending on Xbox Series X|S dropped by 2% and Switch 2 fell by 12%.

It will be interesting to see the November US hardware data when it comes in, as experts have said the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S could get a jolt in sales from people buying systems to play GTA 6. However, Circana has warned that sales might not be as strong as expected due to the increased prices.

Microsoft, Sony, and Nintendo have raised prices on their consoles due in part to the ongoing memory and component shortages from the AI buildout.

Tariffs have also played a role. On the subject of tariffs, all three received refunds from the government after the Supreme Court deemed the tariffs illegal, but those companies are keeping the money and not giving anything back to you. The companies argued that people who paid more knew what they were doing and don't deserve to get any money back.

#3655. GTA 6’s Digital Release Has GameStop CEO Defending Physical Games, For Obvious Reasons

The GTA 6 launch looks set to break several records, as the digital-only game appears on track to be a major critical and commercial hit. Right on cue, GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen has criticized publishers that forgo a traditional physical release as a business strategy that hurts consumers and GameStop's bottom line, without explicitly mentioning GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive.

"When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it, or lend it to a friend," Cohen said to Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all-digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop. Of course they don't like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying new. They're taking away competition."

Cohen's comments come in the wake of GTA 6 being a digital-only release--the "physical" edition includes a download code for it. It's also somewhat ironic for Cohen to defend physical games, given the GameStop boss's July remarks that physical video games were "irrelevant" to GameStop's business strategy. That business model has relied heavily on secondhand game sales, and none of those profits ever made their way back to the original publishers. Currently, GameStop says that selling video game software makes up the smallest part of its business.

But in the case of GTA 6? Going digital probably made financial sense for Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games. The entire game clocks in at over 211GB, which means three standard 100GB Ultra HD Blu-ray discs would have been needed to house GTA 6 in its launch-day entirety--although realistically, Take-Two probably would have opted for one disc and forced consumers to download the rest of the game. That would have raised costs, and it wouldn't be unlikely to imagine Take-Two fearing the discs being reverse-engineered for secrets ahead of GTA 6's launch.

Going digital essentially removed those risks, and while PlayStation and Xbox do take a cut of profits for hosting the game on their servers. According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 sales for PS5 alone have reached $1.38 billion in revenue so far, which means Sony is profiting handsomely from those sales. Retailers are still entitled to a share of the profits for stocking the code-in-a-box version of the game on their shelves, and once you start to factor in distribution costs, Take-Two's reasoning starts to make sense. The publisher says 98% of its business is digital, but it's not ruling out a proper physical GTA 6 edition in the future.

Maggie Coughlan is promoted to global managing editor. Since joining the team in 2021, she has held several positions at Vanity Fair, most recently as executive editor. She previously held editorial roles at the New York Post and People.com. She holds a master’s degree in digital publishing from NYU.

Emily Shugerman joins Vanity Fair as a senior staff writer reporting on wealth and politics on the West Coast. Emily comes from The San Francisco Standard, where she covered the shifting political allegiances of Silicon Valley’s richest, the fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax, and the growing power of AI lab workers. Before that, she was a reporter at The Daily Beast, where her investigations spurred leadership changes at national nonprofits and policy shifts at major corporations. Her work has also appeared in The Cut and The Guardian. She lives in San Francisco.

Jack Holmes joins as a senior editor for Vanity Fair, where he’s been editing features and political coverage since January. He will continue that work and expand into society and technology. Previously he was a senior staff writer and political editor for Esquire. He’s also the founder and publisher of The Football Weekend, a publication covering world soccer. Jack graduated from Vanderbilt University with a degree in philosophy and political science.

Nina Joyce is vice president of communications, based in New York, leading Vanity Fair’s communications globally. With 17 years of experience, she previously oversaw media relations for Condé Nast’s UK business and portfolio of brands, managing corporate reputation, brand strategy and major cultural events. Prior to joining Condé Nast, Nina spent a decade at Vice Media Group, holding senior roles across VICE, Refinery29, and i-D, and ultimately leading corporate PR across EMEA.

Roxanne Doucet joins as global visuals director. She has worked across New York and Paris, and collaborated with renowned artists and luxury houses including Dior, Loewe, and Balenciaga, building a practice rooted in fine art, documentary photography, and editorial storytelling. She was previously visual director at Vogue US and has consulted for Vogue France.

Dondre Stuetley joins Vanity Fair as senior visuals editor. Previously he was the photo editor at WSJ Magazine, commissioning stories on art, fashion, entertainment, design, food, and architecture.

Sameet Sharma joins as senior visuals editor. He was most recently the visuals director at V Magazine, and prior to V, he oversaw visual production at G-III, working on brands such as DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld. He also brings experience from Hearst magazines, where he worked on the photo teams at ELLE, Marie Claire, and Esquire.

Christian Zelaya joins as a senior designer. He brings more than five years of experience shaping editorial reporting into creative and clever visual stories for digital and social platforms and attracting readers for global brands like NBC, Forbes, and Scholastic.

Michael Kanyongolo joins Vanity Fair as audience development manager. He was most recently the news producer for Quanta Magazine, where he carried out web development, visual design, and production. He previously worked on web production at the New York Post and has a background in media and psychology.

Nazanin Hakim joins Vanity Fair as a creative producer on the video team. She brings a background in documentary filmmaking, having worked on a range of projects exploring politics, culture, and technology, including the Emmy-nominated series Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror and What’s Next? The Future With Bill Gates.

Chris Black joins Vanity Fair as a contributing editor. He is a writer, photographer, and cohost of How Long Gone. He lives in New York and Los Angeles.

#3653. Why GTA 6 Doesn’t Include Disney World

Walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida. Many are wondering why, especially when GTA: Vice City had its own parody of the theme park--Fun World--many years ago.

Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson said the decision to came down to resources and story reasons. “A theme park would represent a lot of work that we didn’t have, and we didn’t have a strong narrative reason to send them there,” he told VGC.

Nelson added that Rockstar isn't known to cut corners, so if GTA 6 were to have its own version of Walt Disney World, it would be a "fully functioning theme park," and that just wasn't doable.

Walt Disney World is much more than just its most famous park, Magic Kingdom. The property includes three other main parks, Animal Kingdom, Hollywood Studios, and Epcot, along with the Disney Springs shopping district, multiple water parks and golf courses, and more than two-dozen hotels. The entire property is more than 25,000 acres. Even if Rockstar were to replicate only a portion of the scale of the real Walt Disney World, it would surely be a big job.

Players might expect fully functioning rides, and Nelson said the challenge for Rockstar would be, "Where do you stop? When do you feel like it's enough?"

Nelson said people think Rockstar has unlimited time and money, and that isn't true. "So sometimes you just have to admit we are not going to be able to make this to the level we feel we need to,” he said.

Plus, as Nelson pointed out, there would need to be a story reason to send Jason and Lucia hundreds of miles north from Miami to Orlando, where Walt Disney World is. GTA 6 has a huge map, but it's contained to Vice City and its surrounding areas--it doesn't go that far north.

It’s not difficult to imagine why Jennifer Lopez went viral when turned up to the 2000 Grammys in her green dress with a super low-plunging neckline. (That dress looked like it was made for her!) But did you know that The X-Files and David Duchovny also played a role in why it’s such a moment, too? I sure didn’t!

Most people know that JLo’s green Versace “jungle dress” is such a big celebrity fashion moment that it led to the creation of Google Images. It caused such a high volume of online interest that Google, which was only two years old at the time, decided it was time to engineer the feature. Although The X-Files of it all? I had no idea. Lopez told the story of the dress recently, saying this about it:

I was nominated that night and I wore it to The Grammys, and I was very excited. It was just one of those moments… [I didn’t know it was going to be something], I just picked the best dress on the rack.

JLo didn’t set out to create some internet-shattering moment when she stepped out at the Grammys. She just wanted to look good. As she added on Friends Keep Secrets:

When I walked out on stage you could see it on my face because there was like swell in the room of [applause]. And, I was just like, ‘What’s happening?’ And then, David Duchovny was with me, and he was like, ‘This is the first time in years I know nobody’s looking at me.’

So Lopez presented an award with David Duchovny, who was one of the biggest names in TV at the time, who was in his seventh season of the show. In the clip she talked about how at the time Duchovny couldn’t go anywhere without being recognized and had recently filed a multi-million dollar lawsuit against 20th Century Fox. Here they are together:

I can imagine Duchovny feeling perhaps like the heavily covered lawsuit might be the elephant in the room when he was going to The Grammys that night. However, when he was paired with JLo on the night of the green dress, all eyes were on her. As JLo continued:

The thing is I walked out on stage and it was like a bodysuit, right? And it had the material, very just flowy material, like chiffon. And when I walked out, it blew open. The moment was the thing. The wind blew, the people started, he had the perfect line. It wasn’t scripted.

It sounds like the room absolutely lost it when JLo hit the stage with Duchovny, and his line complimented it all like a cherry on top. Even though the moment happened over twenty-five years ago, it has remained relevant over the years with a number of pop culture moments. The most recent one has to be when Mika Abdalla wore the dress during a scene in Off Campus. (The show’s costume designer shouted out how the dress stayed on if you’re as curious as I was).

And then, Rachel Zoe also put on the dress for a magazine cover shoot, too. Last year, the original model who first wore the Versace piece on the runway, Amber Valletta, also slipped back into the chiffon dress. Will JLo ever top this look? We don’t know, but you can see her in The JLO Show, streaming with a Paramount+ subscription on November 26.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and Rockstar Games has released the game's official map. It is absolutely gigantic.

Even though we knew the GTA 6 map would be big--it has more playable space than GT4, GTA 5, and Red Dead Redemption 2 combined--seeing the map for yourself shows off its truly gargantuan scale.

After GTA 6 reviews came online, shares of Rockstar owner Take-Two ripped higher, but the company is still down massively this year and over the past 12 months.

#3649. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang May Just Survive His Scandal

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Exactly three years ago today, the tech world found itself in an all-too-familiar crisis. On an otherwise ordinary Friday afternoon, the board of OpenAI abruptly fired Sam Altman, following a secretive deliberation about what was believed to be a pattern of deceptive behavior by the CEO. A shock wave of panic rippled through the industry: Employees rallied around Altman, who set up a makeshift war room in his Russian Hill home; investors made furious calls to the board to demand a reversal; and Satya Nadella offered to create the conditions within Microsoft for Altman and his loyalists to rebuild OpenAI from the ground up.

As the members of OpenAI’s board racked their brains for who might make a worthy replacement, the extent of their miscalculation quickly dawned on them. OpenAI could not survive without Altman, and the tech industry might not survive without OpenAI. Within four days of Altman’s firing (an event so fleeting that it came to be known as “the blip”), he was reinstated as CEO, and the board coup that failed to kill him only made him stronger.

Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It would be difficult to overstate Huang’s influence on the AI industry and US tech policy at large.

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.

As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”

Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

#3647. Macaulay Culkin to Star in 'Home Alone' Sequel Written by Seth Rogen: Details

Macaulay Culkin might find himself home alone once again.

Multiple outlets reported on Friday, November 20, that Culkin, 46, is in talks to return to the Home Alone franchise in a sequel developed by Disney and 20th Century Studios. Seth Rogen and his producing and writing partner, Evan Goldberg, are reportedly attached to pen the script, which is based on an idea that Culkin himself pitched to Disney in recent months.

The plot centers on Culkin’s character, Kevin McCallister, as a father, according to Deadline.

Us reached out to reps for Disney for comment.

In July, Culkin was reportedly spotted at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, to discuss the potential film.

“I got a tip the other day that there was a very interesting sighting on the Disney lot: Macaulay Culkin was there,” veteran entertainment journalist Matthew Belloni shared on his “The Town” podcast. “He’s talked about having an idea for a new Home Alone, and Disney is, like, salivating.”

He continued, “They’re offering him another movie — like, he could do his own passion project if he could also do another Home Alone — and they have a good idea. I’ve talked to people who have heard it, and it’s a really good idea for a Home Alone reboot with Macaulay Culkin.”

As a child, Culkin starred in the original 1990 comedy directed by Chris Columbus. The classic holiday movie follows 8-year-old Kevin, who is accidentally left alone at his parents’ home in Chicago while his family heads off on a Christmas vacation in Paris. Kevin must fend for himself and defend his home when a pair of burglars attempts a robbery.

Culkin reprised his role in the 1992 sequel, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which finds Kevin alone in New York after he accidentally boards the wrong plane.

Home Alone and Home Alone 2, also directed by Columbus, grossed a combined $836.3 million. The franchise spawned a 1997 threequel without Culkin, instead starring Alex D. Linz and directed by Raja Gosnell. The third film grossed $79.1 million worldwide.

A fourth made-for-TV installment, Home Alone 4, recast Kevin (Mike Weinberg) and was directed by Rod Daniel in 2002. A 2012 made-for-TV film, Home Alone: The Holiday Heist, starred Christian Martyn as Finn Baxter. The installment was directed by Peter Hewitt.

The franchise’s most recent installment, Home Sweet Home Alone, arrived on Disney+ in 2021, directed by Dan Mazer and starring Archie Yates as Max Mercer.

“It’s been revisited with really bad sequels. Sorry to insult anybody, but they’ve completely f***ed it up,” Columbus, 68, told The Hollywood Reporter in December 2025 while celebrating the original film’s 35th anniversary. “It started with Home Alone 3, and then it just went downhill from there; Home Alone 3 is sort of the best of the bunch of the bad movies.”

Culkin also shared his idea for a reboot.

“I like the idea that maybe Kevin’s older, that he’s like a widower or something like that. He’s raising his kid and they don’t really get along, he’s working all the time. … it’s almost like a Liar, Liar kind of thing,” he told the outlet. “There’s one of two ways you can do it. One, he actually leaves the kid behind by mistake; he calls up his mom like, ‘So sorry, I get it now.’ Or I leave him behind on purpose, like, ‘Oh, that made me the man I am today.’”

Spoilers for I Play Rocky are ahead! You can catch the movie in theaters now.

When I think about the best sports movies, often the big match or game at the center of it comes to mind immediately. For instance, with Rocky, the titular character’s fight with Apollo Creed is something I instantly picture when the film gets brought up. So, I was surprised to see the fight wasn’t really featured within the story of I Play Rocky, the project on the 2026 movie schedule about the making of Rocky. Instead, it was used during the credits.

It turns out there is a reason why that big match was cut from the film and moved into the credits.

Now, even though they took a “week” to film the fight between Rocky and Creed for this movie, it was eventually cut…kind of. Ultimately, the scene was moved to the credits. So, why did that happen? Well, director Peter Farrelly told me the match was actually supposed to be the end of I Play Rocky. However, a big realization about the stairs scene changed his mind, as he recalled during an interview with CinemaBlend:

And by the way, it wasn't originally supposed to be over the end credits. It was supposed to be the end of the movie. But when you get in an editing room, as good as the script is, you have to let the movie find its way. And when he goes up the top of those stairs [and raises his arms up], there was such a high watching it that you couldn't get there again.

While the director was very open about this being the right call with me, he also admitted that it took him a while to fully accept that. It took a long time to film the fight, and it’s such an iconic moment from Rocky. However, he eventually came to the conclusion that they had to move it to the credits:

Like even though we took a lot of time making that fight and doing it, you will never get that high again. You're not going to feel it. And so I showed it to a few people in the editing room. They go, ‘You should end on the top of the stairs.’ I was like, ‘No, I took a week. I took a week to shoot the fight. I'm not cutting the fight.’ And it took me a couple weeks to finally realize I have to cut the fight. It's got to end on the stairs.

I know I was a bit shocked not to see the fight prominently featured in the movie, when so many of the other scenes are. However, I did think it was a cool surprise to cut it into the credits, and it served as a full-circle moment to the scene where we watch Anthony Ippolito’s Sylvester Stallone and Stephan James’ Carl Weathers train for the fight.

Speaking of Ippolito and James, they, like Stallone and Weathers, trained and learned how to box for this movie. That means they took a few punches too. When I asked the Sly actor about filming the fight between Rocky and Creed, he said:

We took some real we took some real shots during that. Me and Stephan were just trying to figure it out, and you know, sometimes we messed up here and there, and we tag each other, but it was all right.

James also confirmed that they took some hits while preparing for and filming this movie. He revealed that he and Ippolito trained together as well, and “got close in a very short period of time,” noting that they were “in the trenches with each other.” That became very clear too, as he told me:

I may have taken a punch or two that I wasn't looking forward to. But you know, had to do what I had to do to pull it off. And I think it was all worth it that we were able to, you know, not only step into these guys psychologically, but physically as well.

Well, considering the amount of time, effort and punches that went into this, I’m happy that Rocky and Creed’s fight did find its way into the movie…even if it wasn’t in the way it was originally intended.

Now, if you’d like to see how this legendary sequence is shown in the credits of the well-reviewed I Play Rocky, you can catch the film in theaters now. And if you’d like to compare their take on the sequence to Rocky’s, you can stream the OG movie with a Paramount+ subscription.

#3644. Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?

Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

$7 billion: That’s how much Sound Ventures, the firm founded by actor turned VC Ashton Kutcher and former music manager Guy Oseary, stands to profit from its 0.5% stake in Anthropic after the IPO this week.

#3643. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3641. Mom and Caregiver Let Boy, 3, Die From Treatable Cancer by Skipping Treatment

A mother and caregiver were arrested after they allegedly let a 3-year-old boy with curable cancer die by skipping two years of treatment that would have saved his life.

Destiny Schliefert and Debbie Sue Potter were arrested on Wednesday, November 18, and were both charged with second-degree murder, abuse or neglect of a child resulting in death, and four counts of first-degree child endangerment, according to court records viewed by Us.

Both Schliefert and Potter are currently in custody at the Christian County Jail.

Doctors noticed a cyst on the boy’s left kidney when he was born on June 1, 2023, according to their probable cause statements viewed by Law & Crime.

In March 2024, the boy was diagnosed with neuroblastoma, which is a rare cancer of immature nerve cells. The type of cancer is most common in infants.

Authorities said that the child’s last recorded visit to a medical center in Kansas City, Missouri, with his mother, Schliefert, was on May 14, 2024. Schliefert allegedly stopped bringing her son in for treatment after doctors advised her to return every 12 to 24 weeks for additional assessment and treatment.

The doctor who previously saw the boy said his neuroblastoma “was survivable” if it was treated “with proper care,” according to Schliefert’s probable cause statement.

The boy reportedly went to a different hospital in Clinton, Missouri, for treatment, nearly one year later in April 2025. He allegedly weighed just over 23 pounds at the time, and the visit appeared to be his last time he saw medical professionals.

Schliefert and her son moved into a home in Ozark, Missouri, with Potter in July 2025. Potter was identified as “grammy” in court documents, and she took on caregiver responsibilities.

Authorities said that the boy’s condition rapidly weakened. Schliefert has been accused of being aware of her son’s condition, and she reportedly searched for the “fastest way to get a toddler to gain weight fast” and “bulk up a toddler fast” in July, per the court documents.

One day after Schliefert made her final search regarding her son’s health, the Ozark Police Department reported to the family’s home when they received a report that a boy who was “unresponsive and not breathing.” The boy was ultimately pronounced dead at the scene.

First responders “were very concerned and expressed suspicions of child abuse, based on the physical appearance of the child who passed away,” according to the probable cause statements. Additionally, police said the boy “appeared to be severely malnourished, undersized, obviously weak and dirty,” looking like a “third world starved child” and “having no muscle to his arms and legs.”

An investigation was launched into the matter, and police reportedly found the boy’s body in a bedroom while “completely covered with a black and red ‘AC/DC’ blanket.” Additionally, there were “several cockroaches, and other bugs” crawling around the boy’s exposed food and hand.

Authorities determined that the home was filthy and “unsafe for children.”

An autopsy was later conducted on the boy, which found “bumps” on his rib cage that “appeared to be tumors.” The autopsy also determined that his official cause of death was “metastatic neuroblastoma in the setting of medical negligence,” and the manner of death was ruled as homicide.

A detective spoke with Schliefert on Wednesday, and she reportedly claimed that doctors told her her son would live a “long happy life.” She also claimed she called to reschedule appointments at the Kansas City hospital, but “the hospital never called her back.” (The doctor who treated the child rejected her version of events.)

Schliefert allegedly told officers that her son had his last doctor’s appointment in August 2025 and claimed she didn’t take him to see doctors due to her lack of medical insurance.

While speaking to authorities, Potter acknowledged that the adults in the home were concerned about the child’s health. However, she insisted he was “still eating, drinking, and playing” and never appeared to be sick.

It’s not currently clear if either Schliefert and Potter have entered pleas following their arrests. The Ozark Police Department did not immediately respond to Us’ request for comment regarding updates in the case.

#3640. How WoW: Forever Is Overhauling Classic WoW’s Infamous PvP Honor Grind

World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs. player systems will work much differently than in previous versions of old-school WoW, developer Blizzard has revealed.

While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch. Now, Blizzard has shared more information about how players will earn PvP ranks and honor, with the main takeaway being that players won't have to commit to months of grinding or competing with players on their own faction for top ranks.

Honor, a currency earned from killing enemy players and completing battlegrounds and PvP activities, will now exclusively be used to purchase PvP gear and doesn't impact progress towards ranks. Instead, players will rank points by completing daily and weekly PvP quests, fighting in open-world PvP activities like the Gurabashi Arena, and competing in the weekly battleground.

In a video detailing the new system, Blizzard said the rank climb will now feel "more varied and predictable" than in the past, when players needed to farm varying amounts of Honor to rank up based on how other players on their same faction were performing. It will also encourage players to engage in different PvP activities each week, instead of simply doing the most efficient one in terms of Honor gained. 

Though it isn't central to ranking up, Honor still remains as a currency and is used to purchase  PvP gear. Players can start purchasing PvP gear at lower ranks, and then use Honor to upgrade those items into epics once they've reached higher ranks. At the max rank of 14, players unlock access to epic weapons equal in power to gear from the MMO's endgame raids. 

Blizzard said the biggest way to progress the ranks is by completing weekly season journey quests. For those who might be unable to play for a few weeks and worry about falling behind, each weekly quest doesn't disappear and can be completed later in the season. 

Forever's PvP rank grind will still take several months of dedicated play (according to Blizzard, players can expect to hit max rank by week eight or nine of a season), but the amount of actual time required will be far less. That's thanks to players on the same faction no longer competing to farm the most Honor in order to achieve top ranks, something that resulted in players of original WoW and WoW Classic grinding battlegrounds for 12 or more hours a day for months on end.

"WoW: Forever's Honor system keeps you coming back each week, rather than grinding every day," Blizzard said. "We hope this is a more approachable system that still provides a healthy challenge as you climb to max rank."

This isn't the first time Blizzard has revamped classic WoW's Honor system. Though it kept the infamous old system in place for WoW Classic's launch in 2019, it finally made changes in 2023. It kept the Honor grind somewhat intact, but removed the competition between players on the same faction, instead requiring players meet certain Honor thresholds each week to rank up.

Forever looks to be a hit for Blizzard so far, with more than 15 million characters created and a record breaking number of concurrent, returning, and weekly players. Despite the game's massive launch and a banner year for WoW in general, it wasn't enough to snag the MMO a nomination for Best Ongoing Game at The Game Awards. 

In other Forever news, Blizzard recently hotfixed a major dungeon exploit that saw some players, including prominent streamers, earn thousands of gold, only for Blizzard to then remove the ill-gotten gains and issue temporary account suspensions to the worst offenders.

#3639. The Nightingale First Look: Dakota and Elle Fanning on Their Long-Awaited First Film as Sisters

When I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” says Dakota, who’s in New York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value costar Stellan Skarsgård. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”

Now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” says Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”

The Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”

Dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” says Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, says she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complementary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”

Morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”

Of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who, after reading the 2015 historical novel, told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne shows her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” says Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”

Although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”

Their director says because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them, and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”

The Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” says Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” says Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”

But they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” says Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”

“It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar-winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”

Morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her costars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn’t grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”

Hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s important historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”

It wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position, and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”

“Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew, and they were grinning from ear to ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”

Hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”

Nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”

To hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets, and I’ve seen her work,” says Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”

“But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she says, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”

#3638. What Happened to Sonia Exelby? Woman Killed by Man She Met in Fetish Chatroom

A British piano tutor’s shocking death at the hands of a self-described “alpha sadist” she met in an online fetish chatroom has ended with a Florida jury delivering a unanimous verdict, two consecutive life sentences and gut-wrenching statements from her family in court.

Dwain Hall was found guilty on November 20, 2026, of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby in October 2025. A jury of 12 deliberated for roughly an hour before telling Judge Timothy McCourt they’d reached their decision, concluding that the murder was premeditated. Hall was sentenced immediately to two consecutive life sentences in prison.

The case drew international attention after Exelby — a music tutor from Portsmouth, England — flew across the Atlantic to meet a man she had only known online. What followed was a horrifying sequence of events that prosecutors described as a sadistic exploitation of a vulnerable woman struggling with severe mental illness.

Here’s everything to know about Sonia Exelby’s death, the investigation and the trial that ended with Hall behind bars for life.

Exelby flew from London to Gainesville, Florida, on October 10, 2025, where Hall picked her up from the airport. The pair then traveled to an Airbnb in Reddick, Florida, according to court documents obtained by Us.

When Exelby failed to board her return flight to England on October 13, 2025, authorities in the United Kingdom considered her endangered and missing. U.K. officials called on the Florida Department of Law Enforcement to help investigate her disappearance.

As the search unfolded, investigators turned up disturbing evidence on Exelby’s computer. According to Hall’s arrest affidavit, the materials indicated “she was suicidal and traveling to the United States to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered.”

On October 17, 2025, Exelby’s remains were discovered buried in a shallow grave in Marion County. Hall, who lived in Ocala, was arrested on murder and kidnapping charges about a month later, on November 17, 2025. He later pleaded not guilty. Inside Dwain Hall’s Online Connection to Sonia Exelby Hall admitted to investigators that he and Exelby had met on a fetish website and had been communicating for roughly two years before she traveled to Florida. According to the affidavit, he said the two “discussed bondage, suicide, and her desire to have someone kill her.”

Hall’s profile on the website — which has since been taken down in the U.S. — described him as a “sadist,” according to The Times. One of the sites where they connected, motherless.com, allowed anonymous users to upload disturbing images of women and children being tortured, raped and killed. The website is now defunct.

Hall also told police that Exelby had promised to pay him $4,000 to kill her, framing the arrangement as a consensual contract. But evidence presented at trial painted a very different picture of what happened inside that Airbnb.

While staying at the rental, Exelby sent frantic messages to a friend over Discord that suggested she was reconsidering the deadly arrangement — and that she was afraid.

“I’m sorry he keeps taking my phone he doesn’t trust me with it,” she wrote in messages included in the affidavit. “He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night. I can’t kill anyone.”

She continued, “I’m so so scared I’m so broken and in so much pain all I can do is lay here and doing what [he] wants makes him respect me enough not to do the things I really hate. Everything but some are.”

A video Hall recorded of Exelby inside the Airbnb on October 11, 2025, showed bruises and abrasions on her body, according to the affidavit. The next morning, the Airbnb’s owner received a notification that Exelby had checked out of her stay — days before her body was recovered.

“Hall knew Exelby suffered from severe mental illness and was suicidal,” the affidavit states. “He claimed that he wanted to help Exelby and did not want her to die but his actions show differently. Exelby was in a foreign country and extremely vulnerable.”

Hall’s trial began in Marion County on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Assistant State Attorney Amy Berndt told jurors that Hall had targeted Exelby “because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure,” per The Independent.

“And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body,” Berndt continued.

Prosecutors argued that Hall didn’t try to save a struggling woman — he preyed on her. After just about an hour of deliberation, the jury agreed, returning a unanimous guilty verdict and finding the murder was premeditated. Hall, who was 53 at the time of his conviction, was sentenced on the spot to two consecutive life sentences.

Eight of Exelby’s family members were in the courtroom to hear Hall’s fate, and four of her siblings delivered statements before his sentence was handed down.

“Dwain, you pretended to care for Sonia,” Barry Wilton said in court, per the Daily Mail. “But you didn’t at all. You used her for your sick fantasy. You had the opportunity to save her. Instead, you took her from us. May your actions weight heavily on your mind for the rest of your pitiful life.”

Luke Wilton praised the Florida officials who handled the case and the strangers who supported the family during the painful proceedings.

“This year has been terrifying for the family. We were terrified coming here. What we found, however, is decency and care. People met here were stunning, seeing how the state of Florida fought for us, seeing all these people came here together in harmony for us,” he said.

Luke added, “Thank you to the jury for their patience and attentiveness, and to the prosecutors who left nothing to chance, and staff who looked after us for kindness, humanity and dedication.”

Ahead of the trial, Exelby’s sister Gemma Isaj created a GoFundMe to help the family cover travel costs to Florida. On the page, Isaj remembered her sister as “a beautiful, gentle and incredibly kind soul” who “struggled with her mental health.”

“Her struggles were only one part of her story,” Isaj wrote. “Sonia was so much more than the difficulties she faced. She was a loving sister, aunt, daughter, family member and friend.”

#3637. You Can Play Grand Theft Auto 6 At 60fps Using This Absurdly Complicated Method

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out for consoles, and it's every bit the visual showcase of the generation that it was promising to be since its reveal. You'll struggle to find a better-looking game on the current generation of hardware, but one concession Rockstar had to make to achieve that was limiting its frame rate--a limitation some players are going to absurd lengths to overcome.

Irrespective of what platform you play on, Grand Theft Auto VI is limited to 30fps. Doubling that to the more desirable 60fps is something current console hardware just isn't capable of with this level of visual fidelity and simulation, which means you'll have to rely on other methods of frame generation to get there. That's the idea that underpins technology like Veyra: an open-source real-time video enhancer that uses your PC and HDMI 2.1 capture card to bring frame generation to your console.

It's a...complicated process. First you'll need a capable capture card (like one of the many from Elgato) that is able to ingest gameplay at 4K over HDMI 2.1. You'll need to connect that to your PC using certified USB-C 3.2 data cable, which needs to plug into a suitable motherboard with True USB 3.2 Gen 2 support. On the pricier end of the requirements, you will need a relatively powerful GPU, with the creators recommending a RTX-40 or newer card from Nvidia in order to tap into the card's Tensor cores (that are used for frame generation on PC). Pair that with an OLED monitor, which is also strongly recommended thanks to its near-instant pixel response times, and you've got everything you need to finally enjoy Grand Theft Auto VI (and more) at higher frame rates.

Veyra is able to take gameplay captured on your console and apply a variety of enhancements over the footage, which is ultimately displayed (and played) through the PC you're capturing the footage to. You can utilize upscaling and frame generation techniques from Nvidia, AMD, and Intel to enhance both the resolution and perceived fluidity of your console games this way, with as minimal latency as possible. Given all the parts in the chain, from your console, to the capture card, and through to your PC, escaping any additional latency is impossible. But Verya is seemingly built with mitigating latency as its highest priority, and seems to achieve that based on feedback from some users on Reddit.

Is it worth it to go through this much hassle to play GTA 6 at 60fps? If you have all the required hardware then it's at least worth a shot, even just for the sake of curiosity. But actually investing in a setup to achieve this is probably overkill. For starters, it requires a PC that will probably be capable enough to play Rockstar's latest sequel at or on-par with the console version once it does land on PC (which will reportedly be sooner than you think). Capture cards are not outrageously expensive, but they're also not free, which can also be said for all the high-quality cables you'll need between each of the three required devices.

I admit, I admire the dedication to playing Grand Theft Auto VI at launch in the best possible way, but I would wager that you're likely going to be spending a lot more time troubleshooting some incompatibility somewhere along this chain of dependencies instead of enjoying the game itself. Still, if you're curious you can find a lot of detailed information about what this setup requires and why, and determine for yourself if it's worth the price to cruise around Leonida with a bit more fluidity.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, on the 2026 TV schedule, only just debuted as the first spinoff, and immediately had its own drama. Funnily enough, the biggest drama of the season involved O.G. Mormon Wives star Mayci Neeley, who got dragged into the mix when older sister McCall DaPron clashed with some of the new cast members.

Things quickly escalated when McCall made Mayci aware of some drama with co-star Bobbi Althoff, resulting in a text to Jen Affleck saying, “I’m gonna f*** them up,” in regard to the individuals who clashed with her sister. And then, Jen told everyone what Mayci said. After it all became public, it was suddenly so much bigger than just venting between sisters, making someone who had previously been thought of as one of the most grounded and level-headed of the original Mormon Wives series come across like a mean girl.

I’m sure we’ve all said things in a text in the heat of the moment, but Mayci’s words got out for all to see, leading her to realize her mistake in responding in the heat of the moment. She also expressed real regret for having made the statement at all. In a recent apology statement, she said:

To be honest, I’m embarrassed. I’m genuinely embarrassed that I said that. I don’t remember the intention behind it because I know I wasn’t trying to get into a street fight, like a physical fight. It’s genuinely embarrassing. I don’t know why the hell I said that.

Even though the text did make me look at Mayci a bit differently from the impression I’d gotten of her on The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, I also understand wanting to defend a family member and don’t blame her for having a strong reaction to feeling like her sister was being attacked. It all felt a bit middle school, and I’m certainly not making ay excuses for her over-the-top response, but the firsthand experience with some wild drama on her own reality TV series probably led Mayci to have a more heightened reaction than she might otherwise have had.

Anytime you get a group of people together who come from different backgrounds, have them spend long periods of time together, and point cameras at them, you’re bound to get some drama as they get to know each other. It was a bit unusual that this particular drama came from someone not actually in the room where it happened, but it sounds like Mayci has definitely learned a lesson from the fallout. She went on to say:

I am very sorry I said that. I did regret saying that. That is definitely out of character for me. … I’m just going to be accountable for the things that I was upset with myself for. I’ve apologized for it, and moving on.

Largely because of Taylor Frankie Paul, we’ve become accustomed to Mormon Wives being synonymous with drama, especially with the chaos surrounding production of the original series. After the cancellation of her season of The Bachelorette, custody issues with her children, and her announced departure, it immediately turned attention to the new spinoff and the drama in the OC. So, I’m glad that Mayci didn’t seem to waste any time in sharing such an honest reaction to her own behavior.

While we don’t yet know the future of this new series, fellow Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt is getting her own reality show. You can check out The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives and its Orange County spinoff with a Hulu subscription while we await news of future seasons, other possible spinoffs, and more headline-making drama.
